overview: The file contains a Department of State cross-reference to a September 1935 despatch transmitting John Carter Vincent’s report on the Kwantung Leased Territory, followed by an October 1936 consular despatch from Dairen about the thirtieth anniversary of the Kwantung Government. The latter describes ceremonies at Port Arthur attended by senior Japanese and Manchukuo officials and uses the occasion to assess Japanese colonial administration, especially its limited provision of education for the territory’s Chinese population and its efforts to strengthen ties between Japan and Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Atcheson despatch transmitting Vincent’s Kwantung report
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to another file for George Atcheson Jr.’s despatch transmitting John Carter Vincent’s report on the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: This filing note refers to despatch material located under file number 894C.01/84. The referenced despatch was sent from Nanjing by Atcheson on September 12, 1935, and transmitted a report prepared by John Carter Vincent, formerly consul at Dairen. The report itself is not included in this file.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the thirtieth anniversary of the Kwantung Government
subfiles.from: Stuart L. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Erle R. Dickover, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grummon reports on the Port Arthur commemoration of thirty years of Japanese government in the Kwantung Leased Territory and discusses colonial education for the Chinese population.
subfiles.summary: Grummon reports that the thirtieth anniversary ceremony was held at Port Arthur on October 1, 1936, after being postponed from September 1 because that date coincided with the anniversary of Japan’s 1923 earthquake. Senior Japanese and Manchukuo officials attended, and speakers presented the territory as a historical and economic link between Japan and Manchukuo. Grummon identifies education of the local Chinese population as a conspicuous failure of Japanese administration and reproduces Takebe’s statement that only about thirty percent of Chinese children received schooling. Takebe also announced additional spending in the Kwantung Bureau’s 1937 budget to expand educational facilities and reinforce the proclaimed indivisibility of Japan and Manchukuo.

interest: The file juxtaposes a pointer to Vincent’s broader 1935 survey with a focused eyewitness account of colonial commemoration in 1936. Grummon’s despatch is especially useful for its list of attending Japanese and Manchukuo dignitaries, its account of the political symbolism attached to Port Arthur, and its reproduction of official educational statistics. Its language also reveals contemporary American diplomatic perceptions of Japanese colonial rule and the racialized economic and social roles imposed on the territory’s Chinese inhabitants.
